sections.h2: Does Ohio charge an estate tax?
sections.html:
No. The Ohio Department of Taxation says the state estate tax was repealed for people who died on or after January 1, 2013, through House Bill 153 of the 129th General Assembly. A later sunset in House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly reached older deaths as well: no Ohio estate tax is due on property first discovered after December 31, 2021, or on property found earlier but never disclosed or reported before that date.

For a family planning to sell an inherited house in Ohio, the practical result is that no state estate tax return stands between the heirs and a closing. The Department also states that it no longer requires the tax release or inheritance tax waiver forms (ET 12, 13 and 14) before a decedent's assets pass to someone else, and it has asked county auditors and banks to stop sending those forms in.

sections.h2: Could the federal estate tax reach an Ohio estate?
sections.html:
Only a large one. The IRS lists the federal basic exclusion amount at $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026, a change made by the law signed July 4, 2025 (Public Law 119-21). A single house rarely comes near that line, so for most families selling one property the federal return is not what drives the timeline.

The IRS also says an estate that is not required to file a federal estate tax return should not file Form 8971, and that the estate of a person survived by a spouse may elect to pass along unused exclusion to the spouse on a timely filed return. The table below shows the exclusion by year of death as the IRS prints it.

Federal basic exclusion amount by year of death, per the IRS

sections.h2: Can heirs sell an inherited Ohio house before probate is finished?
sections.html:
Usually the executor or administrator is the one who signs, and the probate court where the decedent lived supervises. Ohio's land sale procedure for executors, administrators and guardians sits in Revised Code sections 2127.01 through 2127.43, and an executor whose will grants a power of sale may proceed under the will instead.

Small estates can skip full administration. Under R.C. 2113.03 a probate court may release an estate from administration when its assets are worth $35,000 or less, or $100,000 or less when everything goes to a surviving spouse by will or by intestacy. The court can then order real property transferred to the people entitled to it and may appoint a commissioner to sign the conveyance documents. Such an order frees real property in the hands of an innocent purchaser for value from possible claims of unsecured creditors, just as administration would.

  • Ask the probate court clerk whether the estate qualifies for release or needs letters of authority.
  • Collect the death certificate, the will if there is one, and the vesting deed for the house.
  • Order a title search early so liens and unpaid taxes show up before a buyer finds them.

sections.h2: What if the owner recorded a transfer on death affidavit?
sections.html:
Then title may already belong to the named beneficiary. R.C. 5302.22 lets an Ohio owner designate who receives a house at death by signing a verified transfer on death designation affidavit and recording it with the county recorder before the owner dies. When it is properly recorded, title vests in the beneficiary or beneficiaries named in the affidavit at the owner's death.

The affidavit needs no payment and no delivery to the beneficiary to work, and the recorder charges the same fee as for a deed. Heirs who think a parent signed one should ask the county recorder to search the owner's name, because the recorder indexes the affidavit under the owner of record. A person who knowingly makes a false statement in the affidavit commits falsification under R.C. 2921.13.

sections.h2: What tax do heirs face when they sell an inherited Ohio house?
sections.html:
Gain is measured from the heir's basis, and for inherited property the IRS says that basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death. An estate that chose the alternate valuation date uses that value, and special-use valuation can apply to farm or business real estate. Publication 551 adds that if no Schedule A (Form 8971) arrives from the executor, the heir can use the appraised value at the date of death for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

The practical step is to get a date-of-death appraisal early and keep it with the estate papers. A tax preparer can then apply it to the sale price.

Ohio also lets each county levy a real property transfer tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, set by county commissioners. R.C. 322.02 puts that charge on the grantor, to be paid to the county auditor before the deed goes to the recorder. Ask the county auditor for the rate in the county where the house sits.

  • Date-of-death appraisal or Schedule A value, for the basis.
  • Letters of authority or a release order, for the right to sign.
  • County auditor transfer tax rate, for the closing statement.

sections.h2: Can heirs still contest the county's value of an inherited Ohio house?
sections.html:
Yes, the owner can. R.C. 5715.19 lets a property owner, the owner's spouse, or a qualified representative file a complaint with the county auditor against the valuation of a parcel. The complaint is due on or before March 31 of the ensuing tax year or the date the first-half collection closes, whichever is later, and the county board of revision hears it. The statute generally bars a second complaint on the same parcel in the same interim period unless something changed, such as an arm's length sale, casualty loss or substantial improvement.

A fresh date-of-death appraisal can support a complaint when the county value looks high. Ask the county auditor how to obtain the complaint form and which tax year it covers.

sections.h2: What should an Ohio heir do first?
sections.html:
Start with the paperwork that decides who may sign, then move to the property itself. Ohio's process depends on the county where the decedent lived, so the probate court clerk is the first call.

  • Locate the original will and file it with the probate court if it has not been filed.
  • Secure the house, keep insurance active, and forward the mail.
  • Ask the county recorder whether a transfer on death affidavit was recorded.
  • Request a copy of the tax bill from the county treasurer to see what is owed.
  • Get a date-of-death appraisal for the basis.

sections.h2: How do heirs sell an inherited Ohio house as-is?
sections.html:
Many heirs live out of state, and a house that needs work is hard to stage and show. Selling as-is means the buyer takes the property in its current condition and the estate skips repairs, which can shorten the time the estate carries utilities, insurance and property tax.

Whatever route the estate chooses, the legal steps above still apply: the person with authority signs, the county auditor handles the transfer tax, and the deed goes to the county recorder. If you want a cash offer on an inherited Ohio house, the number to compare is the net amount the estate receives after those costs, not the headline figure.

faqs.q: Does Ohio have an estate tax in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The Ohio Department of Taxation reports that the estate tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2013, and the 2021 sunset in House Bill 110 ended collection on older estates for property first discovered after December 31, 2021.

faqs.q: Do I need a tax release from the state before transferring my parent's Ohio house?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Taxation says it no longer requires the ET 12, 13 or 14 release forms before certain assets of a decedent move to another person. Title and probate steps still apply, so ask the county probate court what the estate needs.

faqs.q: Is there a federal estate tax on a modest Ohio estate?
faqs.a: Not at that size. The IRS puts the federal basic exclusion amount at $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths, and an estate below it is not required to file Form 706 on that basis. The figure was $13,990,000 for 2025.

faqs.q: Can a house pass without probate in Ohio?
faqs.a: A recorded transfer on death designation affidavit can vest title in a named beneficiary at the owner's death under R.C. 5302.22. A small estate may also be released from administration when assets are $35,000 or less under R.C. 2113.03. Check which applies with the probate court.

faqs.q: Who pays the county transfer tax when an estate sells a house in Ohio?
faqs.a: The grantor pays it. R.C. 322.02 says the tax is levied on the grantor named in the deed and paid to the county auditor before the deed is presented to the recorder, at a rate each county sets up to thirty cents per hundred dollars.
